claims.text: Retention of a single-phase solid solution in equimolar or near-equimolar multimetal nanoparticles is governed by the balance between mixing enthalpy and thermally activated atomic diffusion.
A sufficiently negative mixing enthalpy stabilizes the single-phase solid solution.
Strong chemical interactions among the constituent metals can counter tendencies to form intermetallic phases or segregated precipitates.
Increasing temperature increases atomic mobility in the nanoparticles.
Increased atomic mobility can overcome enthalpic stabilization and cause intermetallic-compound formation or phase separation.
The operando catalytic atmosphere can influence atomic diffusion and phase evolution.
When atmospheric composition does not induce phase changes, temperature is the primary variable mediating diffusion and segregation.
If mixing enthalpy sufficiently stabilizes the alloy, XRD and TEM will show retention of the original single-phase structure across most of 473–1923 K.
Sufficient enthalpic stabilization will yield stable catalytic performance across most of 473–1923 K.
Sufficient enthalpic stabilization will yield stable thermoelectric performance across most of 473–1923 K.
At the high end of the temperature range, thermal energy can exceed stabilizing chemical interactions and produce phase separation or intermetallic phases.
Phase separation or intermetallic formation will cause catalytic or thermoelectric performance degradation.
Highly oxidative environments can cause deviations from the predicted thermally governed behavior.
Elemental combinations with especially favorable intermetallic formation energies can deviate from the predicted single-phase stability.
The temperature threshold for segregation depends on the specific elemental composition.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis permits complete single-phase retention when chemical stabilization is sufficiently strong, but the falsification rule also treats retention across the entire range as falsifying. Without an independently specified mixing-enthalpy or diffusion criterion, the same observation can therefore be interpreted as either confirmation or falsification.
